cases.abstract: Exact attention can avoid storing a quadratic attention matrix and still leave substantial GPU compute capacity unused. FlashAttention-2 targets this remaining inefficiency by changing both the arithmetic and the distribution of work in tiled attention. It delays output normalization to reduce non-matrix operations, distributes sequence blocks across thread blocks to improve occupancy, and assigns query rows to warps so that forward outputs require no inter-warp reduction. These changes preserve softmax attention without approximation and retain linear additional memory in sequence length. On A100 attention benchmarks spanning sequence lengths of 512 to 16k with a fixed total of 16k tokens, the implementation is 1.7-3.0 times faster than FlashAttention. Training 1.3B- and 2.7B-parameter GPT-style models on eight A100 GPUs yields gains of up to 1.3 times over FlashAttention and reported throughput of 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU. For multi-query decoding, a separate partitioning strategy spreads key-value cache loading across thread blocks, making the attention kernel up to seven times faster than FasterTransformer. The results distinguish improvements to individual kernels from the smaller gains available in full-model training.
cases.methods: FlashAttention-2 assigns different query rows to different warps while making each key and value tile available to all of them. Because attention normalizes each query row separately, a warp can compute its rows of scores and their value-weighted outputs without summing partial outputs produced by other warps. The earlier split-key arrangement instead required shared-memory writes, synchronization, and reductions. Independent query-row blocks also run on separate thread blocks, increasing available parallel work when a small batch or few heads would otherwise leave GPU multiprocessors idle. Within each row block, online softmax accumulates an unnormalized output, rescales it when the running maximum changes, and applies the accumulated denominator only after the final key tile. This reduces normalization work while retaining exact softmax attention. Saving rowwise log-sum-exp permits probabilities to be recomputed during backpropagation rather than storing the quadratic attention matrix.
cases.results: The end-to-end measurements show that context length changes how much the faster attention kernel matters. On eight A100 80GB GPUs, the 1.3B GPT-style model rises from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context when replacing FlashAttention with FlashAttention-2, but from 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B model similarly moves from 189 to 205 at 2k and from 175 to 225 at 8k. Thus, the largest training gain over FlashAttention is about 1.3-fold, despite attention-kernel gains of 1.7-3.0-fold across the training benchmarks; accelerating one operation does not multiply whole-model throughput equally. The standard PyTorch attention benchmark also runs out of memory at 16k, whereas the tiled implementations complete that setting. The reported peak 72% model FLOPs utilization uses the conventional training formula without halving causal attention FLOPs, so it should be read as an accounting-based utilization measure rather than a direct count of executed operations.
cases.notes: Prioritized work partitioning and the difference between kernel and training gains. Decoding comparisons concern the attention kernel, not complete generation latency. The utilization convention is retained in the results interpretation. Prospective hardware-specific optimizations and longer-context extensions are not treated as completed findings.

cases.abstract: Autoregressive decoding repeatedly invokes a large model even when available hardware could evaluate several candidate continuations concurrently. Speculative decoding uses a cheaper model to propose a short token sequence and lets the target model check its prefixes in parallel. A probability-based acceptance rule retains valid proposals, while a residual distribution corrects the first rejection; this produces exactly the target sampling distribution for any approximation model, without retraining or changing the target architecture. Analysis relates accepted proposals to distributional overlap and predicts walltime gains from the balance between acceptance rate and proposal cost, assuming independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long outputs, and parallel target evaluations that do not lengthen a target step. In batch-one tests on a single TPU-v4, a 77M-parameter T5-small draft model accelerates an 11B-parameter T5-XXL model by 2.6 times for English-German translation and 2.3 times for summarization under standard sampling. Greedy decoding reaches 3.4 and 3.1 times, respectively. Larger draft models accept more proposals but run more slowly overall. The speedup therefore depends on spare computational capacity and cheap, sufficiently accurate proposals, rather than reducing arithmetic work.
cases.methods: At a given prefix, let p and q be the target and draft token distributions after applying the desired sampling rule. A draft token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). If rejected, its replacement is sampled from the normalized positive part of p - q. Accepted proposals contribute probability mass min(p(x), q(x)); the rejection branch supplies exactly the missing target mass, so their sum is p(x). The decoder checks draft prefixes in parallel, stops acceptance at the first rejection, and applies this correction there. If all proposals pass, it samples an extra target token. Each iteration therefore produces between one and gamma + 1 tokens. With independent, identically distributed acceptance rates of mean alpha, the expected token count is (1 - alpha^(gamma + 1))/(1 - alpha). This yield measures reduced serial target calls, not necessarily reduced computation.
cases.results: Better agreement with the target does not necessarily make a draft model faster in use. For English-German translation at batch size one on a single TPU-v4, greedy T5-XXL decoding with T5-small has an acceptance rate of 0.75 and achieves a 3.4-fold walltime speedup over the T5X baseline. T5-large raises acceptance to 0.82, yet yields only 1.7-fold speedup with the same seven-token draft length. The added draft cost outweighs the improved acceptance. With T5-small, moving from greedy to standard sampling lowers translation acceptance to 0.62 and speedup to 2.6-fold; summarization shows the same direction, from 3.1-fold to 2.3-fold. These comparisons favor a cheap proposal model rather than the most accurate one among those tested. The broader GPT-like and LaMDA evaluations measure acceptance, not implemented walltime gains. Moreover, rejected continuations waste target computations: the method exploits concurrency and can increase arithmetic operations, so these latency gains do not establish lower computational cost.
cases.notes: Separated exact distribution preservation from the assumptions used to predict speed. Walltime evidence is limited to the implemented T5 experiments; other model families supply acceptance measurements. Did not generalize the T5 sampling comparison to every model or present the oracle-based adaptive-drafting bound as an implemented improvement.
